title: Alpha Diversity
text: Alpha diversity measures diversity within single sample. ecodive, metrics grouped four categories based aspect diversity quantify.

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Richness metrics estimate number distinct features (e.g., genera) sample. simplest metric, observed(), counts features non-zero abundance. Chao1 estimator extends inferring number unobserved, low-abundance features based ratio singletons (counts == 1) doubletons (counts == 2).
code: # Equivalent to rowSums(counts > 0) observed(counts) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool  #>      4      3      4      5 # Infers 8 unobserved genera chao1(c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 5, 5, 5)) #> [1] 16  # Infers less than 1 unobserved genera chao1(c(1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5)) #> [1] 8.125  # Datasets without 1s and 2s give Inf or NaN chao1(counts) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool  #>    4.5    3.0    NaN    Inf

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Diversity metrics account richness evenness (equally abundances distributed). Simpson’s index often used measure evenness, representing probability two randomly selected individuals belong different species. Shannon diversity index (entropy) another common metric weights richness evenness.
code: # High Evenness (0.8) vs Low Evenness (0.07) simpson(c(20, 20, 20, 20, 20)) #> [1] 0.8 simpson(c(100, 1, 1, 1, 1)) #> [1] 0.07507396  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(simpson(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.02302037 0.18806133 0.50725478 0.63539593 # High richness, High evenness shannon(rep(100, 100)) #> [1] 4.60517  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(shannon(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.07927797 0.35692121 0.74119910 1.10615349

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Dominance metrics focus abundance common species. Berger-Parker index proportional abundance single abundant feature.

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Given: n : Number features (e.g. species, OTUs, ASVs). X_i : Integer count -th feature. X_T : Total counts (sequencing depth). X_T = \sum_{=1}^{n} X_i P_i : Proportional abundance -th feature. P_i = X_i / X_T F_1 : Number singletons (X_i = 1). F_2 : Number doubletons (X_i = 2).

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Given: r : Rare cutoff (features \le r counts considered rare). F_{rare} : Number rare features. F_{abund} : Number abundant features (> r counts). X_{rare} : Total counts belonging rare features. C_{ace} : Sample abundance coverage estimator. \gamma_{ace}^2 : Estimated coefficient variation. C_{ace} = 1 - \frac{F_1}{X_{rare}} \gamma_{ace}^2 = \max\left[\frac{F_{rare} \sum_{=1}^{r}(-1)F_i}{C_{ace}X_{rare}(X_{rare} - 1)} - 1, 0\right] D_{ace} = F_{abund} + \frac{F_{rare}}{C_{ace}} + \frac{F_1}{C_{ace}}\gamma_{ace}^2

code: I am analyzing the [PACKAGE_NAME] R package to compare the number of ecologically relevant alpha and beta diversity metrics it provides. The package's reference manual is attached.   Please act as an expert in ecological bioinformatics. Carefully read the manual and adhere to these rules:  1. DEFINITION OF A SUITABLE METRIC:    - ECOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Only include metrics used to quantify community diversity. This includes measures of richness, evenness, dominance, turnover, or nestedness.    - SYMMETRY REQUIREMENT: Strictly ignore any asymmetric metrics (where $d(a, b) \neq d(b, a)$). All included beta diversity metrics must be symmetric.    - EXCLUSIONS: Do NOT count accessory functions, data manipulation, plotting functions, or general statistical correlations (e.g., Pearson/Spearman) unless they are explicitly implemented as a community diversity or dissimilarity index.  2. DISTINCTNESS RULE:    - ARGUMENTS AS METRICS: If a single function computes different named metrics based on a character argument (e.g., `method="bray"` vs `method="jaccard"`), each valid method counts as a SEPARATE metric.    - NAMED METRIC SELECTORS: If a numeric parameter (like q, alpha, or p) is used to dial in specific named indices (e.g., q=0 for Richness, q=1 for Shannon, q=2 for Simpson, or phylogenetic equivalents like Faith's PD, Allen's H, and Rao's Q), count each named case as a distinct metric. Do not count intermediate or arbitrary numeric values.    - THE BINARY TOGGLE: Treat the presence-absence version and abundance-based version of the same metric as ONE entity, unless they are provided as separate functions or separate named methods in a list.    - UNIFRAC EXCEPTION: Count unweighted, weighted, weighted normalized, generalized, and variance-adjusted UniFrac as separate metrics if explicitly supported.  3. CATEGORIZATION:    - ALPHA DIVERSITY: Metrics that quantify the diversity of a single sample or site (inventory diversity).    - BETA DIVERSITY: Metrics that quantify the difference or dissimilarity between a pair of samples (differentiation diversity).  To ensure accuracy, format your response as follows:  - **Candidate Extraction:** List all potential diversity functions and their associated methods/parameters found in the manual. - **Evaluation:** Filter the candidates against the "Symmetry," "Ecological Relevance," and "Distinctness" rules. - **Categorized Metric List:** Provide a table or list of all validated metrics with two columns: [Metric Name] and [Category (Alpha or Beta)]. - **Final Summary:**     - **Total Alpha Diversity Metrics:** [Integer]     - **Total Beta Diversity Metrics:** [Integer]     - **UniFrac Metrics Present:** [Yes/No]

text: Simulated data let us compare every method truth. Forty stool samples, 20 controls 20 treated, contain 150 taxa (ASVs). treated group five abundant taxa bloom 8-fold taxa 6–10 drop 4-fold, absolute terms; 140 taxa don’t change. sample “sequenced”: composition sampled random depth 5,000–40,000 reads, sequencer .
code: library(ecodive)  set.seed(42) n_taxa <- 150 groups <- rep(c('control', 'treated'), each = 20) n      <- length(groups) taxa   <- sprintf('ASV%03d', seq_len(n_taxa)) samples <- sprintf('S%02d', seq_len(n))  # Typical absolute abundance of each taxon: heavy-tailed, sorted so that # ASV001 is the most abundant. base <- sort(exp(rnorm(n_taxa, mean = 0, sd = 2)), decreasing = TRUE)  # True fold changes in absolute abundance (treated vs control). fold <- rep(1, n_taxa) fold[1:5]  <- 8      # blooms fold[6:10] <- 1 / 4  # declines changed    <- fold != 1  # Absolute abundances: the group effect, plus biological noise, plus # patchy absences of the rarer taxa. absolute <- t(sapply(groups, function (g) {   mu <- if (g == 'treated') base * fold else base   mu * exp(rnorm(n_taxa, 0, 0.5)) })) patchy <- matrix(runif(n * n_taxa) < 0.3, n, n_taxa) patchy[, 1:20] <- FALSE absolute[patchy] <- 0 dimnames(absolute) <- list(samples, taxa)  # Total microbial load (e.g. cells per gram), which in a real study would # have to be measured separately. load <- rowSums(absolute)  # Sequencing: draw reads from each sample's composition. depth  <- round(runif(n, 5000, 40000)) counts <- t(sapply(seq_len(n), function (i) rmultinom(1, depth[i], absolute[i, ]))) dimnames(counts) <- list(samples, taxa)  counts[1:5, 1:6] #>     ASV001 ASV002 ASV003 ASV004 ASV005 ASV006 #> S01   8584   1695   4009   1480   1236    461 #> S02   7078   4514   1776   1924   1166    705 #> S03   3198   2471   1677   1102   1150    571 #> S04   6436   3919   3026   2170    959   1674 #> S05   4966   1842   2315   2375    618   1273 mean(counts == 0)  # proportion of zeros #> [1] 0.3563333  # Taxa found in at least 90% of samples, for the steps that need them. prevalent <- colMeans(counts > 0) >= 0.9 sum(prevalent) #> [1] 20

title: Ordination
text: plsda(), partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), finds components count table best separate known groups: PLS regression dummy matrix groups, scikit-learn’s PLSRegression mixOmics::plsda() compute . microbiome counts, norm = 'clr' (pseudocount) usual choice. vip attribute ranks features importance separation.  lda(), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), finds Fisher’s discriminant axes: along groups furthest apart relative variation within , MASS::lda() computes . needs samples features, suits measurements, taxa microbiome table. microbiome tables, distances, use capda(): canonical analysis principal coordinates (CAP; Anderson & Willis 2003), discriminant analysis first m axes pcoa(). chooses m number axes classifies samples correctly left turn, reports success, tests separation groups permutation, BiodiversityR::CAPdiscrim() . capscale(), constrained ordination (db-RDA) similar name. oplsda(), orthogonal PLS-DA (OPLS-DA), separates two groups along one predictive axis, p1, puts table’s variation, unrelated groups, orthogonal axes o1, o2, …, pyopls ropls::opls() compute . predictions one-component PLS-DA; rotation makes plot easier read. r2x r2y attributes give variance table, groups, model explains.  supervised ordination always separates groups given: looks exactly , features samples finds separation even random data. PLS-DA, OPLS-DA CAP plot evidence groups differ. Test difference permutation test distances, permanova(), estimate well groups new samples predicted cross-validation.

text: procrustes() rotates, reflects scales one ordination fit another samples, reports far apart still : Procrustes sum squares, m^2. procrustes_test() asks whether agree better chance (PROTEST), vegan::protest() . , Bray-Curtis unweighted UniFrac PCoAs 30 simulated samples six taxa ecodive’s example tree, along gradient favours taxa one end others : rotated UniFrac coordinates result , Bray-Curtis ones fitted target attribute. plot() draws arrow sample’s rotated point target, shows two metrics disagree.
code: set.seed(1) taxa   <- colnames(ex_counts) grad   <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 30) counts <- sapply(seq_along(taxa), function (j) rpois(30, 3 * exp(grad * (j - 3.5)))) dimnames(counts) <- list(paste0('S', 1:30), taxa)  bc <- pcoa(bray(counts), n_axes = 2) uf <- pcoa(unweighted_unifrac(counts, tree = ex_tree), n_axes = 2)  fit <- procrustes(uf, bc, symmetric = TRUE) attr(fit, 'ss') #> [1] 0.4595868  procrustes_test(uf, bc) #> Procrustes randomization test (PROTEST) #>  #> r = 0.7351, p = 0.001, z =  6.67 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Symmetric Procrustes sum of squares (m^2): 0.4596 #> Samples: 30, axes: 2 plot(fit)

title: Performance Guide
text: ecodive engineered high performance, using parallelized C code deliver results quickly minimal memory usage. use cases, can pass data standard R format (like matrix data.frame) get fast results. However, working large datasets—thousands samples hundreds thousands features—can achieve noticeably better performance paying attention format input data. optimizations minimize internal data conversion steps ecodive perform.

what: The Optimal Input: Compressed Sparse Matrices
title: Performance Guide
text: ecodive highly efficient reformatting data internally one-calculations. need manually format data single function calls. However, plan run multiple ecodive functions large dataset, see performance benefit converting data optimal format first. format column-compressed sparse matrix (dgCMatrix) Matrix package, samples arranged columns. conversion , prevent ecodive reformat data subsequent function call.
code: library(ecodive) library(Matrix)  # Assume 'my_counts' is a standard matrix with samples in rows my_counts <- as.matrix(ex_counts)  # Convert once to the optimal format optimal_counts <- as(t(my_counts), "dgCMatrix")  # Now, run multiple analyses on the pre-formatted object. # Remember to specify margin = 2L since samples are in columns. shannon_vals <- shannon(optimal_counts, margin = 2L) simpson_vals <- simpson(optimal_counts, margin = 2L) observed_vals <- observed(optimal_counts, margin = 2L)

title: Performance Guide
text: Many diversity metrics operate transformed data, commonly relative abundances (norm = 'percent'). specify transformation like norm = 'percent', ecodive performs conversion internally. adds small amount computational overhead. plan run many different analyses transformed data, efficient perform transformation pass pre-transformed data ecodive, specifying norm = 'none'.
code: # Inefficient: Transforming the data twice shannon_vals <- shannon(optimal_counts, norm = 'percent', margin = 2L) simpson_vals <- simpson(optimal_counts, norm = 'percent', margin = 2L)  # More Efficient: Transform once rel_abund <- t(apply(t(optimal_counts), 1, function(x) x / sum(x))) rel_abund <- as(rel_abund, "dgCMatrix")  shannon_vals <- shannon(rel_abund, norm = 'none', margin = 2L) simpson_vals <- simpson(rel_abund, norm = 'none', margin = 2L)

title: Performance Guide
text: one exception rule centered log-ratio transformation (norm = 'clr'), used calculating Aitchison distance. standard CLR workflow requires replacing zeros small pseudocount transformation (since log(0) undefined). replacement step instantly turns sparse matrix (mostly zeros) fully dense matrix (zeros), dramatically increases memory consumption. ecodive’s implementation CLR-compatible beta diversity metrics pseudocount-aware. Instead modifying entire matrix memory, C engine applies pseudocount dynamically distance calculation. allows input matrix remain sparse enables algorithm work directly original data pointer without creating massive, dense copy matrix object. Therefore, CLR-based metrics, achieve significantly better performance lower memory usage letting ecodive handle transformation. : :
code: # Best for CLR: Let ecodive handle the transformation dynamically aitchison_dist <- aitchison(optimal_counts, margin = 2L, pseudocount = 0.5) # Inefficient for CLR: Adding pseudocounts creates a dense matrix library(compositions) dense_matrix   <- clr(t(as.matrix(optimal_counts)) + 0.5) # Becomes dense aitchison_dist <- euclidean(dense_matrix, norm = 'none')

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2005: Unweighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: unweighted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: unweighted_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=FALSE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=FALSE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric unweighted_unifrac mothur: unifrac.unweighted() First, transform B presence (1) absence (0) indicators. \begin{align*}  &= \{9, 0, 0, 0, 9, 6, 3, 3\} \\ ' &= \{1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1\} \end{align*} \begin{align*} B  &= \{7, 5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 8, 0\} \\ B' &= \{1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0\} \end{align*} apply formula: \begin{align*} U &= \displaystyle \frac{\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(|'_i - B'_i|)}{\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(max('_i,B'_i))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{L_1(|'_1-B'_1|) + L_2(|'_2-B'_2|) + \cdots + L_n(|'_n-B'_n|)}{L_1(max('_1,B'_1)) + L_2(max('_2,B'_2)) + \cdots + L_n(max('_n,B'_n))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.2(|1-1|) + 0.4(|0-1|) + \cdots + 0.3(|1-0|)}{0.2(max(1,1)) + 0.4(max(0,1)) + \cdots + 0.3(max(1,0))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.2(0) + 0.4(1) + 0.8(1) + 0.5(1) + 0.9(0) + 0.6(0) + 0.7(0) + 0.3(1)}{0.2(1) + 0.4(1) + 0.8(1) + 0.5(1) + 0.9(1) + 0.6(1) + 0.7(1) + 0.3(1)}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.4 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.3}{0.2 + 0.4 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.6 + 0.7 + 0.3}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{2}{4.4}  \\ \\ U &= 0.4545455 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2007: Raw Weighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: weighted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: weighted_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=FALSE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=FALSE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_unifrac \begin{align*} W &= \sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|  \\ \\ W &= L_1|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}| + L_2|\frac{A_2}{A_T} - \frac{B_2}{B_T}| + \cdots + L_n|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|  \\ \\ W &= 0.2|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}| + 0.4|\frac{0}{15} - \frac{5}{15}| + \cdots + 0.3|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|  \\ \\ W &= 0.02\overline{6} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.42 + 0.08 + 0.2\overline{3} + 0.06  \\ \\ W &= 1.14 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2007: Normalized Weighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: normalized_unifrac() R Package abdiv: weighted_normalized_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=TRUE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=TRUE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_normalized_unifrac mothur: unifrac.weighted() \begin{align*}  N &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|}   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {L_1|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}| + L_2|\frac{A_2}{A_T} - \frac{B_2}{B_T}| + \cdots + L_n|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|}   {L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}) + L_2(\frac{A_2}{A_T} + \frac{B_2}{B_T}) + \cdots + L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {0.2|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}| + 0.4|\frac{0}{15} - \frac{5}{15}| + \cdots + 0.3|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|}   {0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}) + 0.4(\frac{0}{15} + \frac{5}{15}) + \cdots + 0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {0.02\overline{6} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.42 + 0.08 + 0.2\overline{3} + 0.06}   {0.21\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.66 + 0.56 + 0.51\overline{3} + 0.06}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac{1.14}{2.326667}  \\ \\ N &= 0.4899713 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Chen et al. 2012: Generalized UniFrac R Package ecodive: generalized_unifrac(alpha = 0.5) R Package abdiv: generalized_unifrac(alpha = 0.5) R Package GUniFrac: GUniFrac(alpha = 0.5) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric generalized_unifrac -0.5 \begin{align*}  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})^{\alpha}     |\displaystyle \frac       {\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}}       {\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T}} |}   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})^{\alpha}}  \\ \\  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {     L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}}         {\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}}| +     \cdots +     L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}}         {\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T}}|   }{     L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T})^{0.5} +     \cdots +     L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})^{0.5}   }     \\ \\  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {     0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}}         {\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}}| +     \cdots +     0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}}         {\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15}}|   }{     0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15})^{0.5} +     \cdots +     0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})^{0.5}   }     \\ \\    G &\approx \displaystyle \frac   {0.03 + 0.23 + 0.21 + 0.26 + 0.49 + 0.08 + 0.27 + 0.13}   {0.21 + 0.23 + 0.21 + 0.26 + 0.77 + 0.58 + 0.60 + 0.13}   \\ \\    G &= \displaystyle \frac{1.701419}{2.986235}  \\ \\ G &= 0.569754  \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Chang et al, 2011: Variance Adjusted Weighted (VAW) UniFrac R Package ecodive: variance_adjusted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: variance_adjusted_unifrac() qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_normalized_unifrac --p-variance-adjusted \begin{align*}  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_i + B_i)(A_T + B_T - A_i - B_i)}} }   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_i + B_i)(A_T + B_T - A_i - B_i)}} }  \\ \\  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {     L_1\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_1 + B_1)(A_T + B_T - A_1 - B_1)}} +     \cdots +     L_n\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_n + B_n)(A_T + B_T - A_n - B_n)}}   }{     L_1\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_1 + B_1)(A_T + B_T - A_1 - B_1)}} +     \cdots +     L_n\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_n + B_n)(A_T + B_T - A_n - B_n)}}   }     \\ \\  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {     0.2\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}|}     {\sqrt{(9 + 7)(15 + 15 - 9 - 7)}} +     \cdots +     0.3\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|}     {\sqrt{(3 + 0)(15 + 15 - 3 - 0)}}   }{     0.2\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}}     {\sqrt{(9 + 7)(15 + 15 - 9 - 7)}} +     \cdots +     0.3\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15}}     {\sqrt{(3 + 0)(15 + 15 - 3 - 0)}}   }     \\ \\    V &\approx \displaystyle \frac   {0.002 + 0.012 + 0.010 + 0.013 + 0.029 + 0.005 + 0.016 + 0.007}   {0.014 + 0.012 + 0.010 + 0.013 + 0.046 + 0.037 + 0.036 + 0.007}   \\ \\    V &= \displaystyle \frac{4.09389}{4.174402}  \\ \\ V &= 0.9807128  \end{align*}

title: Parallel and Memory-Efficient Ecological Diversity Analysis
text: Analyzing ecological diversity often computational bottleneck, especially large datasets. ecodive addresses providing: High Performance: ecodive written C parallelized using pthreads, making dramatically faster R packages. Benchmarks show can 14,000x faster use 200,000x less memory. Zero Dependencies: package external R dependencies, making lightweight, stable, easy install. also makes ideal secure backend R packages. Comprehensive Metrics: implements 14 alpha 38 beta diversity metrics, including classic phylogenetic-aware methods like Faith’s PD, complete UniFrac family compositional PhILR distance. Ordination Statistics: Ten ordination methods (PCoA, NMDS, UMAP, t-SNE, db-RDA, robust Aitchison PCA, ), biplots, five permutation tests (PERMANOVA, PERMDISP, ANOSIM, MRPP, Mantel), whole analysis needs package. Trusted Results: Every method tested established package replaces, vegan, ape, scikit-bio, scikit-learn, uwot, gemelli. Results identical number threads, random methods take seed. Ease Use: API simple integrates seamlessly popular bioinformatics packages like phyloseq rbiom.

title: Abundance-based Coverage Estimator (ACE) — ace
text: counts numeric matrix count data (samples \(\times\) features). Typically contains absolute abundances (integer counts), though proportions also accepted. cutoff maximum number observations consider "rare". Default: 10. margin margin containing samples. 1 samples rows, 2 samples columns. Ignored counts special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1 cpus many parallel processing threads used. default, n_cpus(), use logical CPU cores.

title: Abundance-based Coverage Estimator (ACE) — ace
text: ACE metric separates features "abundant" "rare" groups based cutoff (usually 10 counts). assumes presence abundant species certain, true number rare species must estimated. Equations: $$C_{ace} = 1 - \frac{F_1}{X_{rare}}$$ $$\gamma_{ace}^2 = \max\left[\frac{F_{rare} \sum_{=1}^{r}(-1)F_i}{C_{ace}X_{rare}(X_{rare} - 1)} - 1, 0\right]$$ $$D_{ace} = F_{abund} + \frac{F_{rare}}{C_{ace}} + \frac{F_1}{C_{ace}}\gamma_{ace}^2$$ : \(r\) : Rare cutoff (default 10). Features \(\le r\) counts considered rare. \(F_i\) : Number features exactly \(\) counts. \(F_1\) : Number features \(X_i = 1\) (singletons). \(F_{rare}\) : Number rare features \(X_i \le r\). \(F_{abund}\) : Number abundant features \(X_i > r\). \(X_{rare}\) : Total counts belonging rare features. \(C_{ace}\) : sample abundance coverage estimator. \(\gamma_{ace}^2\) : estimated coefficient variation. Parameter: cutoff integer threshold distinguishing rare abundant species. Standard practice use 10.

Ignored counts special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1 pseudocount Value added counts handle zeros norm = 'clr'. Ignored normalization methods. See Pseudocount section. pairs combinations samples distances calculated ? default value (NULL) calculates -vs-. Provide numeric logical vector specifying positions distance matrix calculate. See examples. clust Whether cluster samples (rows columns) returning distance matrix: NULL (default) FALSE keep input order, one stats::hclust()'s linkage methods, "average" (UPGMA), "complete", "single", "ward.D", "ward.D2", "mcquitty" (WPGMA), "median" "centroid", "pcoa" order along first axis pcoa(). Clustering reorders samples result, labels (samples without names labelled positions input): order attribute gives one's position input, meta[attr(d, "order"), ] lines metadata . ecodive's ordinations tests put samples back input order analysing , give metadata usual order. packages see reordered matrix: give metadata reordered order, matched name. matrix's display list keeps clust (FALSE "none"; see ecodive_display), plot.ecodive_dist() follows: NULL clusters samples heatmap ("average"), "none" keeps order. clust needs every distance, used pairs. rho_p()'s similarities clustered \(1 - \rho_p\). cpus many parallel processing threads used. default, n_cpus(), use logical CPU cores.

title: Aitchison distance — aitchison
text: Aitchison distance defined : $$\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^{n} [(\ln{X_i} - X_L) - (\ln{Y_i} - Y_L)]^2}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute counts \(\)-th feature. \(X_L\), \(Y_L\) : Mean log abundances. \(X_L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{=1}^{n} \ln{X_i}\). \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- log((x + pseudocount) / exp(mean(log(x + pseudocount)))) y <- log((y + pseudocount) / exp(mean(log(y + pseudocount)))) sqrt(sum((x-y)^2)) # Euclidean distance

title: Best Subset of Environmental Variables (BIOENV) — bioenv
code: # 30 samples, with five environmental variables; pH and N shift     # the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     env <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       ph    = runif(30, 6, 8),       n     = runif(30, 0, 10),       p     = runif(30, 0, 10),       k     = runif(30, 0, 10),       depth = runif(30, 0, 5) )     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (env$ph - 6) + env$n / 2)      dm <- bray(counts)      # The best subset of each size.     res <- bioenv(dm, env)     res #> # A data.frame: 5 × 3 #> # BIO-ENV #>    size variables          correlation #>   <int> <chr>                    <dbl> #> 1     1 ph                       0.395 #> 2     2 ph, n                    0.575 #> 3     3 ph, n, k                 0.509 #> 4     4 ph, n, k, depth          0.412 #> 5     5 ph, n, p, k, depth       0.3 #> # Attributes: best, method, metric, partial, n_subsets     plot(res)       # Only some variables, transformed, with subsets of up to two.     bioenv(dm, env, ~ ph + log(n) + p, max_vars = 2) #> # A data.frame: 2 × 3 #> # BIO-ENV #>    size variables  correlation #>   <int> <chr>            <dbl> #> 1     1 log(n)           0.457 #> 2     2 ph, log(n)       0.665 #> # Attributes: best, method, metric, partial, n_subsets      # Removing the effect of depth.     bioenv(dm, env, ~ ph + n + p + k, given = 'depth') #> # A data.frame: 4 × 3 #> # BIO-ENV (partial) #>    size variables   correlation #>   <int> <chr>             <dbl> #> 1     1 ph                0.396 #> 2     2 ph, n             0.577 #> 3     3 ph, n, k          0.51 #> 4     4 ph, n, p, k       0.372 #> # Attributes: best, method, metric, partial, n_subsets

code: x <- ex_counts[1,]; p <- x / sum(x) y <- ex_counts[2,]; q <- y / sum(y) sqrt(sum((sqrt(p) - sqrt(q)) ^ 2))

title: Horn-Morisita dissimilarity — horn
text: Horn-Morisita dissimilarity defined : $$1 - \frac{2\sum_{=1}^{n}P_{}Q_{}}{\sum_{=1}^{n}P_i^2 + \sum_{=1}^{n}Q_i^2}$$ : \(P_i\), \(Q_i\) : Proportional abundances \(\)-th feature. \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,] y <- ex_counts[2,] z <- sum(x^2) / sum(x)^2 + sum(y^2) / sum(y)^2 1 - ((2 * sum(x * y)) / (z * sum(x) * sum(y)))

title: Jensen-Shannon distance — jensen
text: Jensen-Shannon distance defined : $$\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left[\sum_{=1}^{n}P_i\ln\left(\frac{2P_i}{P_i + Q_i}\right) + \sum_{=1}^{n}Q_i\ln\left(\frac{2Q_i}{P_i + Q_i}\right)\right]}$$ : \(P_i\), \(Q_i\) : Proportional abundances \(\)-th feature. \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,]; p <- x / sum(x) y <- ex_counts[2,]; q <- y / sum(y) sqrt(sum(p * log(2 * p / (p+q)), q * log(2 * q / (p+q))) / 2)

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) — lda
text: Method Let \(X\) normalized table, \(m_k\) mean group \(k\) (\(n_k\) samples, prior \(\pi_k\)), \(\bar{x} = \sum_k \pi_k m_k\). \(W\) pooled within-group covariance (sample minus group's mean, divisor \(n - g\)) \(B\) -group covariance \(\sum_k n \pi_k (m_k - \bar{x})(m_k - \bar{x})^T / (g - 1)\) (default priors, \(n \pi_k = n_k\)), discriminant axes \(\) maximize \(^T B / ^T W \), ratio -group within-group variance scores (Fisher 1936). eigenvectors \(W^{-1} B\), ratios eigenvalues, eig. axis scaled pooled within-group variance scores 1, scores \((x - \bar{x})^T \), every sample \(x\). scikit-learn's "svd" solver, \(W\) \(B\) never formed: axes come SVD within-group residuals (feature scaled within-group standard deviation), spheres \(W\), SVD weighted group means sphered space. Axes whose singular value \(10^{-4}\) times first dropped, references . Singular tables LDA needs \(W\) invertible: samples features plus groups, feature constant within every group linear combination others within groups (relative abundances add 1 ). Otherwise lda() stops error (scikit-learn MASS::lda() drop null directions warning, axes report depend rounding). Microbiome tables far taxa samples, use capda() instead: canonical analysis principal coordinates (Anderson & Willis 2003) runs LDA first axes pcoa(), choosing many well classify samples, tests separation groups permutation. capda(dm, groups, n_pcoa_axes = 5) gives scores lda(pcoa(dm, n_axes = 5), groups). axes pca() also work. Validate separation LDA supervised: looks directions separate groups, plots separate , readily plsda()'s, even groups differ. read plot evidence difference. Test permutation test distances, permanova(), estimate error rate classifying new samples cross-validation. Matching MASS scikit-learn lda() gives scores, scaling, group means proportion trace MASS::lda() predict(), sign axis, eig square svd. scikit-learn's LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(solver = "svd") divides within-group covariance \(n\) rather \(n - g\), transform() scores scalings_ larger \(\sqrt{n / (n - g)}\); explained_variance_ratio_ prop. priors add 1 rescaled warning; error. names packages MASS::lda() shares name ecodive's lda(), MASS often attached: whichever package attached last masks 's. Write ecodive::lda(), use count_ord(), always runs ecodive's, sure. Elsewhere, "LDA" also means latent Dirichlet allocation (topic models), LEfSe's "LDA score" effect size method. code: # 30 samples along a pH gradient, which shifts the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     ph <- setNames(round(runif(30, 6, 8), 1), rownames(counts))     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (ph - 6))      dm <- bray(counts)      # Are samples that differ more in pH also more different in     # community composition?     res <- mantel(dm, ph)     res #> Mantel test (Pearson) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.593, p = 0.001, z = 9.786 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30     plot(res)       # With rank correlation.     mantel(dm, ph, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z =    10 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # The same as a column of sample metadata.     meta <- data.frame(row.names = rownames(counts), ph = ph)     mantel(dm, 'ph', data = meta, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z =    10 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # Two distance matrices.     mantel(dm, dist(counts[, 6:20])) #> Mantel test (Pearson) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.4893, p = 0.001, z = 6.502 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

code: # 30 samples along a pH gradient, which shifts the first five genera,     # at random locations.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       ph  = round(runif(30, 6, 8), 1),       lat = runif(30, 30, 35),       lon = runif(30, -100, -95) )     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (meta$ph - 6))      dm  <- bray(counts)     geo <- dist(meta[, c('lat', 'lon')])      # Are samples that differ more in pH also more different in     # community composition, beyond the effect of geographic distance?     mantel_partial(dm, 'ph', given = geo, data = meta) #> Partial Mantel test (Pearson) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5931, p = 0.001, z = 9.759 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # With rank correlation.     mantel_partial(dm, 'ph', given = geo, data = meta, method = 'spearman') #> Partial Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z = 9.969 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # The same, through dist_test().     dist_test(dm, 'mantel_partial', 'ph', meta, given = geo, method = 'spearman') #> Partial Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z = 9.969 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

title: Minkowski distance — minkowski
text: Minkowski distance defined : $$\sqrt[p]{\sum_{=1}^{n} (X_i - Y_i)^p}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute abundances \(\)-th feature. \(n\) : number features. \(p\) : geometry space (power parameter). Parameter: power power parameter (default 1.5) determines value \(p\) equation. Special Cases Manhattan distance: \(p = 1\), formula reduces sum absolute differences. Euclidean distance: \(p = 2\), formula reduces standard straight-line distance. Chebyshev distance: \(p \\infty\), formula reduces maximum absolute difference. Base R Equivalent:
code: p <- 1.5 x <- ex_counts[1,] y <- ex_counts[2,] sum(abs(x - y)^p) ^ (1/p)

title: Morisita dissimilarity — morisita
text: Morisita dissimilarity defined : $$1 - \frac{2\sum_{=1}^{n}X_{}Y_{}}{\left(\frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}X_i(X_i - 1)}{X_T(X_T - 1)} + \frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}Y_i(Y_i - 1)}{Y_T(Y_T - 1)}\right)X_{T}Y_{T}}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute counts \(\)-th feature. \(X_T\), \(Y_T\) : Total counts sample. \(X_T = \sum_{=1}^{n} X_i\). \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,] y <- ex_counts[2,] simpson_x <- sum(x * (x - 1)) / (sum(x) * (sum(x) - 1)) simpson_y <- sum(y * (y - 1)) / (sum(y) * (sum(y) - 1)) 1 - ((2 * sum(x * y)) / ((simpson_x + simpson_y) * sum(x) * sum(y)))

code: # 30 samples in three treatment groups. The 'high' group has more     # of the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       treatment = rep(c('ctrl', 'low', 'high'), each = 10),       site      = rep(c('A', 'B'), 15) )     high <- meta$treatment == 'high'     counts[high, 1:5] <- counts[high, 1:5] + 5      dm <- bray(counts)      # Are samples more alike within treatment groups? title: Normalize a Count Table — normalize
text: counts numeric matrix count data (samples \(\times\) features). Typically contains absolute abundances (integer counts), though proportions also accepted. norm transformation: 'percent': Relative abundance: sample's counts divided sum (sum 1). 'chord': sample's counts divided Euclidean norm (squares sum 1). 'hellinger': square root count divided sample's sum (Hellinger transformation). Euclidean distances results Hellinger distances. 'binary': Presence/absence: 1 non-zero count. 'clr': Centered log ratio: \(\log(x + pseudocount)\) minus sample's mean logs, every feature. Zeros get value , result dense. See Pseudocount . 'rclr': Robust centered log ratio: \(\log(x)\) minus mean log sample's non-zero counts, non-zero counts ; zeros stay 0. 'none': transformation. margin margin containing samples. 1 samples rows, 2 samples columns. Ignored counts special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1 pseudocount Value added counts handle zeros norm = 'clr'. Ignored normalization methods. See Pseudocount section. cpus many parallel processing threads used. default, n_cpus(), use logical CPU cores.

title: Normalize a Count Table — normalize
text: normalized table, orientation (samples rows columns, given margin) dimnames counts, form zeros stay zero: base matrix gives numeric matrix. Matrix dgCMatrix, dgTMatrix, dgeMatrix gives class, slam simple_triplet_matrix gives simple_triplet_matrix. Zeros stored. phyloseq, rbiom, SummarizedExperiment object gives normalized count matrix (object), object's orientation. norm = 'clr' always gives dense base matrix, since every zero becomes (usually negative) value, can take far memory sparse input. beta_div(), pca(), envfit() accept norm = 'clr' never make dense copy, prefer can. normalize() warns result \(10^8\) values (800 MB).

title: Normalize a Count Table — normalize
text: pseudocount parameter relevant norm = 'clr'. Zeros undefined centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation. norm = 'clr', pseudocount NULL (default), zeros detected, function uses half minimum non-zero value (min(x[x>0]) / 2) issues warning. suppress warning, provide explicit value (e.g., 1), replace zeros first replace_zeros(), whose result needs pseudocount. matters: choice pseudocount neutral; acts weighting factor can significantly distort downstream results, especially sparse datasets. See Gloor et al. (2017) Kaul et al. (2017) open-access discussions mathematical implications, Costea et al. (2014) impact community clustering. See aitchison references.

code: # Cell counts per gram for each sample of ex_counts.     load <- c(Saliva = 2.0e10, Gums = 4.1e10, Nose = 1.0e10, Stool = 3.2e10)      # Relative abundance x load     q <- qmp_scale(ex_counts, load)     q[1:3, 1:3] #>        Streptococcus Bacteroides Corynebacterium #> Saliva    9391304348   115942029               0 #> Gums     36696388262   185101580               0 #> Nose       217606330    19782394      4925816024     all.equal(rowSums(q), load) #> [1] TRUE      # Vandeputte et al.'s QMP: rarefy to an even sampling depth first     q <- qmp_rarefy(ex_counts, load)     q[1:3, 1:3] #>        Streptococcus Bacteroides Corynebacterium #> Saliva    9391304348   115942029               0 #> Gums     36766619519   173974540               0 #> Nose       232558140           0      4941860465     attr(q, 'sampling_depth')[1:3]  # reads per cell #>       Saliva         Gums         Nose  #> 1.725000e-08 2.160976e-08 1.011000e-07      attr(q, 'target')[1:3]          # reads kept #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  #>    345    707    172       # The load as a column of sample metadata     meta <- data.frame(cells = load, row.names = names(load))     q <- qmp_scale(ex_counts, 'cells', data = meta)      # 16S copy-number correction comes first, as in the authors' script     copies <- seq(1, 4, length.out = ncol(ex_counts))  # per taxon     x <- sweep(ex_counts, 2, copies, '/')     q <- qmp_rarefy(ceiling(x), load)      # Usually followed by Bray-Curtis distances     dm <- bray(qmp_rarefy(ex_counts, load))

title: Robust Aitchison distance — robust_aitchison
text: Robust Aitchison distance defined : $$\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^{n} (X^*_i - Y^*_i)^2}$$ : \(X^*_i\), \(Y^*_i\) : rclr-transformed counts \(\)-th feature. given sample \(X\), \(X^*_i = \ln(X_i) - X_L\) \(X_i > 0\), \(0\) otherwise. \(X_L\), \(Y_L\) : Mean log strictly positive abundances. \(X_L = \frac{1}{|P_X|}\sum_{j \P_X} \ln{X_j}\), \(P_X\) set indices \(X > 0\). \(|P_X|\), \(|P_Y|\) : number strictly positive features respective samples. \(n\) : total number features. title: Squares Richness Estimator — squares
text: Squares estimator defined : $$n + \frac{(F_1)^2 \sum_{=1}^{n} (X_i)^2}{X_T^2 - nF_1}$$ : \(n\) : number observed features. \(X_T\) : Total counts. \(F_1\) : Number features observed (singletons). \(X_i\) : Integer count \(\)-th feature. Base R Equivalent:
code: x  <- ex_counts[1,] N  <- sum(x)      # sampling depth S  <- sum(x > 0)  # observed features F1 <- sum(x == 1) # singletons S + ((sum(x^2) * (F1^2)) / ((N^2) - F1 * S))

title: t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) — tsne
text: Method sample \(\) gets Gaussian distribution samples, \(p_{j|} \propto \exp(-\beta_i d_{ij}^2)\), \(\beta_i\) chosen binary search perplexity (2 power entropy, bits) equals perplexity. input affinities \(p_{ij} = (p_{j|} + p_{|j}) / 2n\). plot, affinities \(q_{ij} \propto (1 + |y_i - y_j|^2)^{-1}\), Student t distribution one degree freedom, whose heavy tail lets dissimilar samples sit far apart. t-SNE moves points \(y_i\) minimize Kullback-Leibler divergence \(\sum p_{ij} \log(p_{ij} / q_{ij})\) gradient descent, momentum per-coordinate gains: momentum 0.5 first 250 iterations, \(p_{ij}\) multiplied early_exaggeration, 0.8. Every 50 iterations, stops gradient's norm \(10^{-7}\), divergence improved 300 iterations (first 250). scikit-learn's defaults. Exact Barnes-Hut gradients exact gradient sums every pair samples, takes time proportional \(n^2\) per iteration. title: ecodive 2.3.1
